newsitem.title: USA: Rights groups say slave labor is rampant in Burma.
newsitem.headline: Rights groups say slave labor is rampant in Burma.

text.p: Burma has forced millions of its citizens into slavery over the past several years in one of the world's worst human rights abuses, several groups charged on Friday.

At a fact-finding hearing that is part of an international investigation, the human rights and labor groups said the military government of Burma, or Myanmar, organized its forced labor system around 1991, mostly to rebuild infrastructure, such as highways and railroads.

"The widespread use of forced labor by the Burmese military regime truly is one of the great crimes of our time, and this hearing contributes to the growing awareness of its dimension and inhumanity," said Phil Fishman, assistant director of the AFL-CIO's International Affairs Department.

The AFL-CIO, a federation of 78 U.S. labor unions, helped prepare a complaint last year by worker delegates to the governing body of the International Labor Organization, which led to the creation of a Commission of Inquiry.
The commission will hold six days of hearings in Geneva in November to examine charges that Burma violated an ILO convention against forced labor that it ratified in 1955.
It is only the ninth time in the ILO's 78-year history that such a panel has been created.

"It is a matter of the gravest concern to the (Clinton) administration and to the Department of Labor," said Andrew Samet, who heads the U.S. Labor Department's Bureau of International Affairs and conducted Friday's hearing.
After the hearing, Samet called Burma's labor practices "one of the most outrageous systematic violations of human rights anywhere in the world today."
Last month President Bill Clinton cited Burma's "severe repression" when he issued an order virtually banning new investment in the country by U.S. citizens and companies.

The United States, the fourth-largest investor in Burma, has halted direct financial aid and blocked much international assistance to the country since the State Law and Order Restoration Council (SLORC) took over in 1988.

Douglas Steele of the International Labor Rights Fund, a Washington-based labor rights organization, estimated that 2 percent of Burma's 42 million to 45 million people was forced to work each day, but up to one-fourth of the population was coerced into labor during some portion of each year.

"Other countries have used forced labor, but not since the concentration camp system of Nazi Germany has a nation instituted such an extensive system, and even that was not part of a global, interconnected economy," Steele said.

He said Unocal Corp., a California-based oil company, was the worst U.S. offender. He accused it and its French partner, Total SA, of being the cause of some forced labor on infrastructure projects related to a $1.2 billion pipeline project that will carry natural gas from offshore Burma to Thailand beginning next year.

Unocal, which defends its Burma investments and says it has helped to improve life in the country, has two lawsuits related to the project pending against it, one by the Burmese government in exile and the other by human rights groups.
